newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government loses support in latest poll.
newsitem.headline: Australian government loses support in latest poll.

text.p: The conservative Australian government's opinion poll lead over its Labor opposition continues to fall, with the gap now down to two points, a newspaper poll published on Tuesday said.
The Australian newspaper's Newspoll also shows dissatisfaction with Prime Minister John Howard rising steadily, supporting separate research into what voters are thinking.
Support for Howard's Liberal-National coalition remained steady over the past two weeks at 42 percent, but Labor's popularity increased three points to 40 percent.

The government's slump comes amid concerns over stubbornly high unemployment, the resignation of a minister over allegations of conflict of interest, and growing dissatisfaction with Howard's performance as the national leader.

Howard remains preferred prime minister over Labor leader Kim Beazley -- 40 percent against 31 percent -- but more people have been unhappy with his performance than satisfied in every Newspoll since May.
The latest poll found 48 percent of those surveyed were dissatisfied with his performance, compared with 40 percent who were happy with it.
This echoes qualitative research by social analyst Hugh Mackay that found even Howard's backers are unhappy with his leadership.
Mackay found Howard's supporters see him as lacking strength and too easily swayed by powerful interest groups and opinion polls.

"Putting together the views of supporters and detractors, the composite picture to emerge is of a man who seems somewhat out of his depth, too easily influenced by the pressure of public opinion and too easily distracted from a clear focus," Mackay said in his annual political sentiment survey.

The latest Newspoll measure of primary support compares with the government's primary vote of 47.3 percent and Labor's 38.8 percent in the March 1996 election, that saw Howard sweep into office and end 13 years of Labor rule.
The coalition's lead hovered around 12 points for almost a year, before dropping steadily over the past few months.
Support for right-wing populist Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party appears to have stabilised around six percent, down from its Newspoll peak of nine percent.
But One Nation -- which opposes immigration, foreign investment and Aboriginal welfare -- remains ahead of the Australian Democrats, the traditional third force in domestic politics.
Democrat support dropped two points over the past fortnight to four percent.
The Newspoll surveyed 1,135 voters around the country by telephone over the past weekend.
